subject: Aligning first-token latency & chunk cadence — proposed targets and next steps
messages:

Cc: Luminate AI Eng <eng-team@luminate.ai>
Date: Sun, 29 Mar 2026 15:05:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Discovery — TTFT / streaming constraints (quick clarifications)

Thanks for the call today, Priyom. Quick clarifications from our side so we can finalize targets for the POC:

- Our primary SLA is user-visible response: ideally TTFT (time-to-first-token) <= 300ms at 95th percentile for single-turn chat.
- For multi-turn sessions, average token throughput per second should sustain ~12 tok/s per session.
- We intend to use SSE for the web UI but could switch to WebSocket if latency demands it.
- Chunk cadence: we'd prefer smaller, more frequent chunks for the typing UX (~80-120 tokens per chunk) rather than a single large burst.

Can your platform guarantee the 95th pct TTFT under bursty traffic (20 concurrent sessions per instance) with our 3k context model? Also, any recommendations re: batching/kv-cache settings to hit those numbers?

Asha
Senior Product Manager
Luminate.ai
From: Priyom Das <priyom.das@redwood.ai>
To: Asha Menon <asha.menon@luminate.ai>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 30 Mar 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Aligning first-token latency & chunk cadence — proposed targets and next steps

Asha — thanks for the clear bullets. Great call. Short recap + proposed next steps below.

Recap of constraints you shared:
- TTFT target: <= 300ms at 95th pct for single-turn on web UI.
- Sustained throughput target: ~12 tok/s per active session (multi-turn).
- Concurrency for POC: up to 20 concurrent sessions per instance, bursty arrival.
- Streaming preference: SSE default; willing to evaluate WebSocket if beneficial.
- Chunk cadence: aim for ~80-120 tokens/chunk for best UX.

Our proposal (high-level):
1) Target SLO: TTFT <= 250ms at 95th pct during warmed KV-cache for the POC. We recommend 250ms (buffer under your 300ms) to avoid SLA misses on spikes.
2) Chunking strategy: initial chunk size 80 tokens, follow-ups 100-120 tokens; enable progressive flushing at 60ms pacing between kernel writes to keep the UI responsive.
3) Transport: start with SSE for simplicity; if experiments show client-side rendering lag at 95th pct we can switch to WebSocket (lower overhead for many small chunks).
4) Instance sizing & concurrency: for your 3k-context model we suggest Dedicated instance type d-gpu-4 for the pilot with autoscaling to cap 20 sessions per instance.
5) Test plan: we'll run a TTFT sweep (cold, warm cache) and a burst concurrency test with your sample prompts.

Next steps:
- Karthik will send a short test plan and required load script by EOD today. (attachment: ttft-test-plan.csv)
- We’ll provision a short Dedicated pilot. Marissa to follow up on contract window.
- Can you confirm a 2-hour slot next week for the pilot run?

I attached a one-page TTFT proposal and the CSV with the initial load script. Happy to sync with your engs.

Thanks,
Priyom Das
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Aligning first-token latency & chunk cadence — proposed targets and next steps

Hi Asha — quick technical notes from our infra perspective. Long version below; TL;DR: targets are achievable with these config choices.

TL;DR
- Hit 250ms (95th) TTFT in warm cache with: prefix/KV warmup, batch size = 1 (streaming), preferential single-token pump, and kernel pacing 50–80ms between flushes.
- For your 20 concurrent sessions per instance: d-gpu-4 with mixed-precision quantization should hold headroom; we’ll instrument token-level latencies.
- Use SSE initially; if you need <150ms 95th, we should try WebSocket + smaller chunk sizes (40–80 tokens).

Detailed notes:
1) Warm vs cold TTFT: cold starts (no KV cached) will be >> target. We’ll run a short prefix warming pass across expected prompt templates before the demo to push sessions into warm state.
2) Batching: streaming workloads need batch=1 to keep TTFT low; we instead rely on KV caching and model compilation to reduce per-token cost.
3) Chunk cadence & pacing: propose 80 tokens first chunk, then progressive 100 tokens. We’ll use an internal pacing loop of 50–80ms between kernel writes to balance throughput vs UI jitter.
4) Network transport: SSE has minimal handshake and is easier for browser integrations. WebSocket reduces per-message overhead for lots of small chunks; we’ll A/B during pilot.
5) Observability: we’ll add token-level histograms, and a TTFT trace for every request. If 95th pct rises >10% during the run, auto-fallback to a slightly larger chunk size and route to higher-tier instance.

I attached the initial load script profile and a sample k6 job we’ll run. Will coordinate exact prompts.

-Karthik
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
